Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 89, verses 1–5:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Fajr

Meccan. Its verses are nineteen.

Al-Nasa'i narrated from Jabir, who said: "Mu'adh led a prayer. A man came and prayed with him, and he prolonged it. So the man prayed in a corner of the mosque and then left. This reached Mu'adh, and he said: 'He is a hypocrite.' This was mentioned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he asked the young man, who said: 'O Messenger of Allah! I pray behind him, and he prolongs it for me. So I left and prayed in a corner of the mosque, and I watered my camel.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Are you causing trials, O Mu'adh? Where are you in relation to (Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High) (By the sun and its brightness) (By the dawn) (By the night when it covers)?'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discourse on the interpretation of His, the Exalted, statement:

[1–5] ﴿By the dawn﴾ ﴿and by ten nights﴾ [al-Fajr: 2] ﴿and by the even and the odd﴾ [al-Fajr: 3] ﴿and by the night when it passes﴾ [al-Fajr: 4] ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾ [al-Fajr: 5]

﴿By the dawn﴾ means the morning, as in His, the Exalted, statement: ﴿And by the morning when it breathes﴾ [al-Takwir: 18]. He, the Exalted, swore by His signs, because of what occurs through it: the ending of the night, the appearance of light, the dispersal of people and all other animals in search of sustenance. That is analogous to the resurrection of the dead from their graves. In it there is a lesson for whoever reflects.

﴿And ten nights﴾ [al-Fajr: 2] are, according to the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, because they are the days of devotion to the rite of Hajj. In al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "No days are there in which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah than these days," meaning the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah.

Ibn Jarir related that it was said that the reference is to the ten days of Muharram. Al-Razi stated the opinion that they are the last ten nights of Ramadan, because in them is the Night of Power, and because it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) "when the last ten [nights] of Ramadan came, tightened his waistcloth, kept his night in worship, and woke up his family." There is another view regarding the ten. It is that they are the nights in which the night becomes utterly dark, its blackness intensifies, and its darkness covers the horizon, and these are five from its beginning and five from its end. The word "ten" is like His statement in the following surahs: ﴿When it covers﴾ [al-Layl: 1] ﴿When it grows still﴾ [al-Duha: 2], which clarifies the aspect of the lesson and makes it most manifest. There is no remoteness in this meaning; rather it is in harmony with the rest of the verses. In sum, the clearest of the specifying interpretations is that which is supported by evidence, strengthened by an indicator, or resembles its counterparts. And Allah knows best.

﴿And by the even and the odd﴾ [al-Fajr: 3] means the created and the Creator. The even refers to all creation, due to its pairing, as in His, the Exalted, statement: ﴿And of everything We created pairs, that you may remember﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 49]. Mujahid said: Everything of Allah's creation is even: the heaven and the earth, the land and the sea, the jinn and mankind, the sun and the moon, disbelief and faith, happiness and misery, guidance and misguidance, night and day.

﴿And the odd﴾ [al-Fajr: 3] is Allah, the Exalted, because it is among His names, and it means the One, the Unique. Thus Allah swore by His essence and His creation. It was also said: the meaning of "by the even and the odd" is all existing things, both essences and attributes, for they are never free of even and odd.

The judge (al-Qadi) said: As for one who interpreted the two as the zodiac signs and the planets, or as the even and odd prayers, or as the Day of Sacrifice and the Day of 'Arafah, perhaps he singled out for mention from the kinds of what is indicated the one he saw as clearest in indicating monotheism, or as a gateway into the religion, or as suitable to what precedes them both.

Ibn Jarir said: The correct position on this matter is to say that Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, swore by the even and the odd, and did not specify one kind of the even or the odd over another kind, by any report or by reason; and every even and every odd is among what He swore by. Whatever the people of interpretation have said, it falls within this oath, due to the generality of His oath by that.

It has been read as "al-witr" with both fatha and kasra on the waw, and they are two dialects.

﴿And by the night when it passes﴾ [al-Fajr: 4], i.e., when it proceeds, as in His statement: ﴿And by the night when it turns back﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 33]. The restriction to this is because in alternation there is a strong indication of complete power and abundant blessing: in the night is rest, which is among the greatest blessings, and in the day are gains and other things. The deletion of the ya' (in yasri) is for lightness and so that the verse-endings correspond. Among the readers are those who delete it, both in pausal and continuous recitation, and among them are those who restrict it to one of the two, as detailed in the books on recitation.

﴿Is there in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾ [al-Fajr: 5] Ibn Jarir said: That is, is there in what I have sworn by of these matters a sufficient proof for one of understanding? What is meant is that in this oath there is enough for whoever understands from his Lord, and it is more severe than swearing in it.

Al-Razi said: The purpose of the interrogation is emphasis, like one who mentions a compelling proof and then says: "Is there in what I have mentioned a proof?" The meaning is that whoever has intellect knows that what Allah, the Exalted, swore by among these things contains wonders and signs of monotheism and lordship. This manner was chosen to humble the creation and to announce the matter's clarity. And (al-Hijr) means intellect, because it restrains its possessor, i.e., prevents him from committing what is not fitting. The object of the oath is omitted, and it is: (you will surely be punished), as His, the Exalted, statement indicates:

The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[15–16] ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honours him and bestows favours upon him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me."﴾ ﴿But when He tests him and restricts his provision for him, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾ [al-Fajr: 15–16]

Then He pointed to man's heedlessness in both states, his wealth and his poverty, and censured his condition in them, with what establishes what preceded regarding his deserving the pouring down of punishment, by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honours him and bestows favours upon him﴾, that is, with wealth and ease. ﴿He says, "My Lord has honoured me,"﴾ that is, has favoured me, on account of the dignity I have with Him.

﴿But when He tests him and restricts his provision for him﴾ [al-Fajr: 16], that is, constricts it for him and makes it scarce, so He does not increase his wealth or widen it for him. ﴿He says, "My Lord has humiliated me,"﴾ [al-Fajr: 16], that is, has abased me through poverty. This is due to the badness of his reflection and the shortness of his vision in both states, for He tested him with wealth so that he would fulfil its duty and recognise God's right in it, and with poverty so that he would display the bearing of chastity and cultivate the character of patience in sufficiency. In every trial and examination, God distinguishes the wicked from the good. Similar to this verse are the verse: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35], and the verse: ﴿Do they reckon that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55] ﴿We hasten to them in good things? **Interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

﴿Never! When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded to powder﴾ [21]. ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ [22]. ﴿And Hell is brought forth that Day. On that Day man will remember, but how will remembrance benefit him?﴾ [23]. ﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life!"﴾ [24]. ﴿On that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾ [25]. ﴿Nor will anyone bind as He binds﴾ [26].

﴿Kalla﴾ ("Never!") is a rebuke to them for that, and a denial of their conduct. What follows it is a warning, by informing about their regret and anguish at a time when regret will not benefit them. ﴿When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded to powder﴾, meaning: pounded again and again, until it becomes scattered dust.

Al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) said: The second ﴿dakkan﴾ is not an emphasis (tawkid). Rather, the repetition indicates comprehensiveness, as in "I read grammar, chapter by chapter (baban baban)" and "The people came, man by man (rajulan rajulan)." Al-dakk (الدَّكُّ, pounding) is close to al-daqq (الدَّقُّ, crushing) in both wording and meaning.

﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ [22]. Ibn Kathir said: That is, the Lord, blessed and exalted, comes to decide the matter, as He wills, and the angels are before Him in rows, row upon row. Ibn Jarir preceded him in this view and supported it with reports from Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra and al-Dahhak: ««Regarding His descent from the sky on that Day, in shadows of clouds, with the angels before Him, and the earth lighting up with the light of its Lord.»»

The approach of the later scholars (al-khalaf) to this is well known: whoever takes the speech to contain an elided noun (hadhf mudaf) for the sake of awe, meaning: His command and His decree come. Or it is a metaphorical analogy (isti'arah tamthiliyyah) for the manifestation of the signs of His power and the clear display of the effects of His dominion and sovereignty.

Al-Zamakhshari said: His state in that matter is depicted as the state of a king who arrives in person. By his presence there appear effects of awe and governance that do not appear by the presence of all his soldiers, ministers and close associates together. End of quote.

It seems that the disagreement between the two approaches is verbal. The approach of the later scholars is based on the principle that the apparent meaning is not intended, and by "apparent meaning" they mean what belongs to created beings and what is impossible for the Creator, so it must be interpreted. As for the early pious predecessors (al-salaf), they deny that the apparent meaning of such words is what belongs to creation. Rather, it is what comes to the mind of the believer who knows that the Essence of the Exalted, just as it is not like other essences, so likewise His attributes are not like other attributes. They are not described in terms of modality (takyif) and cannot be known in any way. Thus they are the true attribution to Him, glorified is He, in a manner befitting Him, like knowledge and power: no likening (tamthil) and no negation (ta'til).

The Imam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Know that some of the later scholars say that the way of the early predecessors is to affirm the attributes as they came, while believing that "their apparent meaning is not intended." This is an ambiguous statement. The phrase "their apparent meaning is not intended" may mean that by the apparent meaning they intend the descriptions of created beings and the attributes of originated things. For example, that God's being "in front of the face of the one praying" means that He is fixed in the wall toward which he prays, or that "God is with us" apparently means He is beside us, and similar things. There is no doubt that this is not intended. Whoever says that the way of the early predecessors is that this is not intended has indeed hit the meaning, but he has erred in asserting absolutely that this is the apparent meaning of the verses and hadiths. This is not the apparent meaning, as I have explained elsewhere. The exception is when this impossible meaning comes to appear to some people, so the one who says that is correct in this respect and excused in this absolute statement, for manifestness and hiddenness may vary according to the states of people, and it is among relative matters. End of quote.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, expanded the discussion of this in al-Risala al-Madaniyya, and clarified that the discussion of the attributes is a branch of the discussion of the Essence. It follows its pattern and takes its example. Thus, if affirming the Essence is affirming existence and not affirming a modality, then likewise affirming the attributes is affirming existence and not affirming a modality.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, also said in some of his fatwas: We say that there is metaphor (majaz) whose evidence is established, and interpretation (ta'wil) that proceeds on the correct path. It is not found in any of our words or the words of anyone among us that we do not say metaphor and interpretation, and Allah is on the tongue of every speaker. But we reject from that what opposes truth and correctness, and what opens the door to demolishing the Sunnah and the Book, and to joining the distorters among the People of the Book. What is transmitted from Imam Ahmad and the majority of his companions is that the Qur'an contains metaphor. Nothing is known of an explicit text on this question from the other imams. Some scholars among his companions and others, such as Abu Bakr ibn Abi Dawud, Abu al-Hasan al-Kharazi, Abu al-Fadl al-Tamimi, and Ibn Hamid, as I think, and others, went to denying that there is metaphor in the Qur'an. What prompted them to that was what they saw of the distortion of the Qur'an by distorters under the claim of metaphor. So they confronted the misguidance and corruption by cutting off its sources. The best of matters is the middle course and moderation. End of quote.

﴿And Hell is brought forth that Day﴾ [23]: that is, it is made manifest, until creatures see it and the disbeliever knows that his destination is to it. Its "coming" is thus a figurative expression (tajawwuz) for its manifestation, as the verse ﴿And Hell is made manifest for whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36] makes explicit. ﴿On that Day man will remember﴾ [23]: his neglect in the world in obedience to Allah and in what brings him closer to Him of righteous deeds. ﴿But how will remembrance benefit him?﴾ [23]: that is, how will its benefit reach him? Or it is a metaphorical analogy (isti'arah tamthiliyyah) for the manifestation of the signs of His power and the clear display of the effects of His dominion and sovereignty.

Al-Zamakhshari said: His state in that matter is depicted as the state of a king who arrives in person. By his presence there appear effects of awe and governance that do not appear by the presence of all his soldiers, ministers and close associates together. End of quote.

It seems that the disagreement between the two approaches is verbal. The approach of the later scholars is based on the principle that the apparent meaning is not intended, and by "apparent meaning" they mean what belongs to created beings and what is impossible for the Creator, so it must be interpreted. As for the early pious predecessors (al-salaf), they deny that the apparent meaning of such words is what belongs to creation. Rather, it is what comes to the mind of the believer who knows that the Essence of the Exalted, just as it is not like other essences, so likewise His attributes are not like other attributes. They are not described in terms of modality (takyif) and cannot be known in any way. Thus they are the true attribution to Him, glorified is He, in a manner befitting Him, like knowledge and power: no likening (tamthil) and no negation (ta'til).

The Imam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Know that some of the later scholars say that the way of the early predecessors is to affirm the attributes as they came, while believing that "their apparent meaning is not intended." This is an ambiguous statement. The phrase "their apparent meaning is not intended" may mean that by the apparent meaning they intend the descriptions of created beings and the attributes of originated things. For example, that God's being "in front of the face of the one praying" means that He is fixed in the wall toward which he prays, or that "God is with us" apparently means He is beside us, and similar things. There is no doubt that this is not intended. Whoever says that the way of the early predecessors is that this is not intended has indeed hit the meaning, but he has erred in asserting absolutely that this is the apparent meaning of the verses and hadiths. This is not the apparent meaning, as I have explained elsewhere. The exception is when this impossible meaning comes to appear to some people, so the one who says that is correct in this respect and excused in this absolute statement, for manifestness and hiddenness may vary according to the states of people, and it is among relative matters. End of quote.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, expanded the discussion of this in al-Risala al-Madaniyya, and clarified that the discussion of the attributes is a branch of the discussion of the Essence. It follows its pattern and takes its example. Thus, if affirming the Essence is affirming existence and not affirming a modality, then likewise affirming the attributes is affirming existence and not affirming a modality.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, also said in some of his fatwas: We say that there is metaphor (majaz) whose evidence is established, and interpretation (ta'wil) that proceeds on the correct path. It is not found in any of our words or the words of anyone among us that we do not say metaphor and interpretation, and Allah is on the tongue of every speaker. But we reject from that what opposes truth and correctness, and what opens the door to demolishing the Sunnah and the Book, and to joining the distorters among the People of the Book. What is transmitted from Imam Ahmad and the majority of his companions is that the Qur'an contains metaphor. Nothing is known of an explicit text on this question from the other imams. Some scholars among his companions and others, such as Abu Bakr ibn Abi Dawud, Abu al-Hasan al-Kharazi, Abu al-Fadl al-Tamimi, and Ibn Hamid, as I think, and others, went to denying that there is metaphor in the Qur'an. What prompted them to that was what they saw of the distortion of the Qur'an by distorters under the claim of metaphor. So they confronted the misguidance and corruption by cutting off its sources. The best of matters is the middle course and moderation. End of quote.

﴿And Hell is brought forth that Day﴾ [23]: that is, it is made manifest, until creatures see it and the disbeliever knows that his destination is to it. Its "coming" is thus a figurative expression (tajawwuz) for its manifestation, as the verse ﴿And Hell is made manifest for whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36] makes explicit. ﴿On that Day man will remember﴾ [23]: his neglect in the world in obedience to Allah and in what brings him closer to Him of righteous deeds. ﴿But how will remembrance benefit him?﴾ [23]: that is, how will its benefit reach him? So what is meant by his remembrance is his regret for his neglect of the righteous deeds that would have granted him the eternal bliss, as His words explain: ﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life!"﴾ [24]: that is, "I wish I had sent forth righteous deeds for this life of mine." Here the lam (ل) is causal, or "I had sent forth at the time of my life," in which case the lam has the sense of "time" (waqt). "Life" here is the life of this world.

﴿On that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾ [25]: that is, no one in the world will punish as Allah punishes.

﴿Nor will anyone bind as He binds﴾ [26]: that is, no one in the world will be bound on that Day as He binds.

It is also recited as "yu'adhdhibu" (يُعَذَّبُ) and "yuthaqu" (يُوثَقُ) in the passive voice.

Al-Samin said: "Adhab" (عَذابٌ) and "withaq" (وِثاقٌ) in the verse stand in the place of "ta'dhib" (تَعْذِيبٌ, punishing) and "ithaq" (إيثاقٌ, binding). The meaning is: no one punishes with a punishment like the punishment Allah inflicts on this disbeliever, and no one binds with a binding like Allah's binding of him with chains and shackles. So "withaq" in the verse means "ithaq," just as "ata'" (عَطاءٌ, gift) means "i'ta'" (إعْطاءٌ, giving).

Then he pointed, by His words, may He be exalted, to what is said to whoever believed and did righteous deeds, in contrast to those mentioned before:

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[27–30] ﴿O soul at rest﴾ ﴿Return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ [al-Fajr: 28] ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ [al-Fajr: 29] ﴿and enter My Paradise﴾ [al-Fajr: 30]

﴿O soul at rest﴾ means: the secure one, whom no fear or grief can disturb. It is the soul whose heart has come to rest through the remembrance of God and obedience to Him, and is kept safe from agitation.

﴿Return to your Lord﴾ [al-Fajr: 28] means: to His promise and His reward.

﴿well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ [al-Fajr: 28] means: well-pleased with what it has been given, and well-pleasing in the sight of its Lord.

﴿Enter among My servants﴾ [al-Fajr: 29] means: join their company, those of whom ﴿there is no fear, nor will they grieve﴾.

﴿and enter My Paradise﴾ [al-Fajr: 30] means: along with them. This saying is either at death, or at the Resurrection, or at entry into Paradise.

Among the strange transmitted interpretations (al-ma'thur, reports handed down from the early authorities) here is the reading of "the soul" as "the spirit" and "your Lord" as "its companion," meaning: return to the body of your companion. This is taken as an indication that the tranquil spirits will be returned to bodies on the Day of Resurrection, and that they have a dwelling before their attachment to the body, in the realm of the malakut (the unseen dominion). The matter is among the obscure questions, indeed among the unseen matters. By knowing the parallel passages of the revelation, the meaning becomes clear after this interpretation.
